items.q: What are the 4 Cs of food hygiene?
items.correct: Cleaning, Cooking, Chilling, and avoiding Cross-contamination.
items.why: Students guess at the Cs. They specifically address the four food-safety risks: dirty surfaces, undercooked food, warm storage, and pathogens transferring between foods (raw to ready-to-eat).

items.q: On a traffic-light label, what does a red light indicate?
items.correct: High amounts of that nutrient per 100g - eat less often.
items.misconception: The food is dangerous and should never be eaten.
items.why: Students treat red as 'forbidden'. Traffic lights are a guidance system - red = high, eat less often or in small portions. Many foods (cheese, olive oil) are red on certain nutrients but fine in moderation.

items.q: Which method of heat transfer cooks food in a microwave?
items.correct: Radiation — microwaves are electromagnetic radiation that makes polar water molecules vibrate, generating heat.
items.misconception: Microwaves cook food from the inside out.
items.why: Microwaves penetrate ~1–2 cm into food and excite water molecules — they cook outer regions first, conducting heat inward. The 'inside out' myth comes from feeling cool outer surfaces after microwaving (because steam carries heat out).

items.correct: No - free-range means the animals had outdoor access; organic adds further rules on feed, land and chemicals.
items.misconception: Yes - any free-range product is automatically organic too.
items.why: Two different certification ideas. Free-range is a welfare/space standard (e.g. hens with daytime outdoor access). Organic standards regulate the whole system - organic feed, no artificial fertilisers or synthetic pesticides, restricted medicines - and usually include outdoor access as well.

items.q: Do only genetically modified foods contain DNA?
items.correct: No - every plant and animal food naturally contains DNA; GM means the organism's genes were deliberately altered.
items.misconception: Yes - ordinary food is DNA-free, and GM food has had genes added in.
items.random_wrong: DNA is destroyed the moment food is picked.
items.why: A famously common misconception in consumer surveys. All cells contain DNA, so all whole foods do too. Genetic modification changes WHICH genes are present or how they are expressed (e.g. pest-resistant maize) - it does not introduce DNA to food for the first time.

items.q: How many portions of fruit and veg a day are recommended?
items.why: It's 5. “10” is the classic near-miss here; knowing why it's wrong is worth as much as knowing the right answer.

items.q: Eatwell Guide is from which country?
items.why: The answer examiners want is: UK. “USA” is the distractor this question was built around — if it tempted you, that's the exact gap to close.

items.q: Recommended portions of oily fish per week?
items.why: The real figure is 1 portion. The wrong options cluster deliberately close — anchor the exact number to one concrete fact so it can't drift.
